chunk_findings.detail: The manual gives two mutually exclusive startup orders. Line 11 says "Call `ddflow_brief` FIRST, before anything else," while line 25 says that if several agents or subagents are present, "call `ddflow_identify` first." In the multi-agent case, following line 11 causes the exact failure the manual itself describes at lines 28-30: identity is derived from the shared worktree, the agents merge into a single identity, `ddflow_brief` answers with someone else's task, and a review gate can compare the agent against itself. An agent in that environment may claim or edit the wrong item.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/prompts/help/manual.md:11 and :25

chunk_findings.detail: The manual instructs that `ddflow_brief` "replaces reading this project's rule and lesson files — do not read those instead," but `ddflow_brief` is described as returning decisions that govern the files about to be touched and lessons ranked for the current task. The manual never restates the global advisory r-ddflow-self-assessment (assess ddflow at the end of every agent run, phase, and before context compaction). An agent that obeys the manual's prohibition on reading the rule files has no remaining source for that required self-assessment and will omit it. This violates the advisory.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/prompts/help/manual.md:13-15 [r-ddflow-self-assessment]

chunk_findings.detail: The compact text “One of several agents: `ddflow_identify` first, or `as_agent` on every call” makes `ddflow_identify` first an acceptable option on the stateless `2026-07-28` revision. On that revision there is no initialize connection, so `ddflow_identify` persists nothing; the old instructions explicitly said to name yourself on every call via `as_agent` or `_meta`. Given multiple agents in one worktree on that revision, an agent calls `ddflow_identify` once and stops; unlabeled later calls are derived from the working tree, identities merge, `ddflow_brief` can answer with someone else’s task, and a review gate can compare the agent against itself and pass.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/prompts/mcp_instructions.md:44

chunk_findings.detail: The unconditional loop “`ddflow_merge`, `ddflow_complete`” removes the PR integration branch. In a project with `[flow].integration = "pr"`, `ddflow_merge` opens the pull request, parks the item IN REVIEW, and releases the lease; the original contract said “do not wait and do not `ddflow_complete` it — take the next item.” The new charter tells that agent to call `ddflow_complete` on a parked item, producing a refusal/confusing loop exactly in the PR-flow case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/prompts/mcp_instructions.md:44

chunk_findings.detail: The "byte cap" is checked with `len(text)`, which counts Unicode code points, not UTF-8 bytes. The previous `mcp_instructions` pipeline line contained `" implement ·"` (U+00B7), so non-ASCII characters can make `len(text) <= 1500` while `len(text.encode()) > 1500`; the same issue is in the unadopted assertion at line 50 and the SessionStart assertion at line 75. Thus the cap this test is meant to enforce is not actually enforced.

chunk_findings.detail: The manual asserts “A plain `ddflow_review` of a gate with a recorded review is a full re-review”, but the same parenthetical states `full=true` is needed when `[review].delta_default` is on—meaning a plain `ddflow_review` is not a full re-review in that configuration. Under `[review].delta_default = true`, an agent following the broad statement will call plain `ddflow_review` expecting the whole diff; the tool actually performs a delta review only (full requires `full=true`), so the full diff is never re-reviewed and a gate can pass with unreviewed changes. The sentence must be qualified: plain is full only when `delta_default` is off; when it is on, plain is delta and `full=true` is required for a full review.

chunk_findings.detail: The cap is measured with `len(text.encode())`, which counts UTF-8 bytes, while the project cap is specified in characters (`<=1.5K chars`, `CHARTER_MAX_CHARS`). chunk_findings.detail: `drift_notes(repo)` always emits “`ddflow adopt --agents claude` refreshes them” for every non-current state, including `edited`. The module’s own contract says a hand edit is kept. Given a repo with a hand-edited `.claude/agents/ddflow-researcher.md`, `states()` returns `{".claude/agents/ddflow-researcher.md": "edited"}`, and `drift_notes()` then falsely tells the user that the command refreshes that file, even though the command is supposed to leave hand edits untouched.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leanagents.py:drift_notes

chunk_findings.detail: The generated implementer role includes `mcp__ddflow__ddflow_wait` in its `tools:` list. This conflicts with [r-lock-cycle-selfheal], which says agents never poll-wait or hold while waiting. If an implementer encounters a dependency or block, it can call that tool and hold, exactly what the rule says ddflow must heal by adding needs edges instead. The role definition should not grant `ddflow_wait` to a non-operator agent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/claude_agents/ddflow-implementer.md:4

chunk_findings.detail: The implementer template defines the role’s full contract but never instructs the agent to perform the end-of-run / phase / pre-compaction ddflow self-assessment required by [r-ddflow-self-assessment]. An agent launched from this file can finish without filing any discovered ddflow bugs, misbehavior, or missing features because no assessment step is present, and the body does not point to a hook that enforces it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/claude_agents/ddflow-implementer.md:8-15

chunk_findings.detail: Both `description` values are unquoted YAML plain scalars that contain `: ` (colon followed by a space): "Read-only ddflow research: gathers…" and "Independent ddflow reviewer: reads…". YAML forbids colon+space inside a plain scalar, so a standard frontmatter parser throws `mapping values are not allowed here`; Claude Code will fail to load either agent definition.

chunk_findings.detail: Both roles state "Never edits files" / "You edit no file", but the `tools:` list includes `Bash`. chunk_findings.detail: The test invokes `run_cli(repo, "adopt", "--agents", "cursor")` but discards the exit code and any stderr, then only checks that `.claude/agents` does not exist. It should first assert the command succeeded and that the intended cursor files were written before asserting no Claude definitions are produced.

chunk_findings.detail: Both roles state "Never edits files" / "You edit no file", but the `tools:` list includes `Bash`. chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to verify that a hand edit is saved by `adopt --agents claude`, but it never checks the saved-edit sidecar or asserts that the edited content (`"Call it whenever"`) exists anywhere after the second adopt. chunk_findings.detail: The new self-assessment instruction still does not tell the agent to check whether a candidate issue is already corrected. chunk_findings.detail: The `description` value is an unquoted YAML plain scalar containing the sequence `: ` (`... end to end: claim ...`). `_front` turns a YAML block list into a Python list, so `tools = [t.strip() for t in str(fm["tools"]).split(",")]` is not a valid parser for the generated templates when `tools:` is written as:

tools:
  - Bash
  - Read

chunk_findings.detail: `"run" in args` treats any Docker argument equal to `"run"` as if it were the Docker `run` subcommand. For an entry `{"command": "docker", "args": ["exec", "worker", "run"]}`, `args.index("run")` returns 2, so the code produces `docker exec worker run -e DDFLOW_MCP_TOOLS=core`. The `-e` ends up after the `CONTAINER COMMAND` position, so Docker passes it as an argument to the container command `run` instead of setting the environment, and the env var is not forwarded to the container.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/workermcp.py:34

chunk_findings.detail: Even for a real `docker run`, the inserted `-e` is placed before existing Docker options. Docker applies repeated `-e KEY=value` options in order and the last one wins. Given `entry = {"command": "docker", "args": ["run", "-e", "DDFLOW_MCP_TOOLS=all", "image"]}` and `tier="core"`, the output is `docker run -e DDFLOW_MCP_TOOLS=core -e DDFLOW_MCP_TOOLS=all image`, so the container receives `all` rather than the configured `core`. The function's `out["env"]` line already overrides an existing env value for non-Docker entries, so the Docker path should likewise win.

chunk_findings.detail: `"run" in args` treats any Docker argument equal to `"run"` as if it were the Docker `run` subcommand. For an entry `{"command": "docker", "args": ["exec", "worker", "run"]}`, `args.index("run")` returns 2, so the code produces `docker exec worker run -e DDFLOW_MCP_TOOLS=core`. The `-e` ends up after the `CONTAINER COMMAND` position, so Docker passes it as an argument to the container command `run` instead of setting the environment, and the env var is not forwarded to the container.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/workermcp.py:34

chunk_findings.detail: Even for a real `docker run`, the inserted `-e` is placed before existing Docker options. Docker applies repeated `-e KEY=value` options in order and the last one wins. Given `entry = {"command": "docker", "args": ["run", "-e", "DDFLOW_MCP_TOOLS=all", "image"]}` and `tier="core"`, the output is `docker run -e DDFLOW_MCP_TOOLS=core -e DDFLOW_MCP_TOOLS=all image`, so the container receives `all` rather than the configured `core`. The function's `out["env"]` line already overrides an existing env value for non-Docker entries, so the Docker path should likewise win.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/workermcp.py:36

chunk_findings.detail: `args[:1] == ["run"]` only recognizes `docker run` when `run` is the first argument. Docker allows global options before the command, e.g. `{"command": "docker", "args": ["--host", "tcp://...", "run", "img"]}`. For that entry with `tier="core"`, the condition is false, so the `-e DDFLOW_MCP_TOOLS=core` forwarding is never added; `out["env"]` only sets the env for the docker client, not the container. Valid `docker run` invocations therefore silently miss the configured tier.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/workermcp.py:worker_entry

chunk_findings.detail: `_without_tier` removes matching `-e`/`--env` pairs from the entire `args[1:]` slice without stopping at the image/command boundary. Example: `worker_entry({"command": "docker", "args": ["run", "img", "mycmd", "-e", "DDFLOW_MCP_TOOLS=all"]}, "core")` returns `["run", "-e", "DDFLOW_MCP_TOOLS=core", "img", "mycmd"]` because `_without_tier` deletes the `-e DDFLOW_MCP_TOOLS=all` arguments. But after `img`, Docker treats those two arguments as the container command's own arguments, not as docker run options, so the function corrupts the container command rather than replacing a forwarded tier. The removal must stop once the IMAGE argument is reached.

chunk_findings.detail: The change still does not fix prior finding #4; it codifies it. The stated intent for this change is that `[session].context_budget_tokens` alias `[session.context_budget].global` and they are the *same value*; conflicting values should be invalid, not silently reduced to the smaller. The new doc line says “if both are set the smaller applies,” directly contradicting that intent, so the invalid config `context_budget_tokens = 40000` plus `[session.context_budget] global = 30000` still silently changes the budget to 30000.

chunk_findings.detail: The new knob documents `0` as “no ceiling at that level” while also defining the effective budget as the smaller of the global and per-type values. Since all values are non-negative and `0` is the sentinel for “no ceiling,” `min(global, type)` is zero whenever either layer is `0`. For example, with `context_budget_tokens = 30000` and `[session.context_budget] claude = 0`, the intended meaning of the per-type `0` is to remove only the claude-specific limit, leaving the global 30000 in effect. But the min formula produces effective budget `0`; because `0` is then interpreted as “no budget,” the global budget is silently disabled for claude. If `0` were instead interpreted as a literal zero-token budget, then the documented global `0` (“no budget”) would zero out every session. Either way the knobs are not independently configurable as the change requires.

chunk_findings.detail: `report` chooses the target for the headline budget from `HR.detect(os.environ)` and ignores the `agent` argument it already receives. If a report is generated for the session whose agent/clientInfo is `agent="claude"` while the ddflow process environment has no recognized harness (`HR.detect` returns `""`), then with `session.context_budget_tokens=1000` and `session.context_budget={"claude": 500}`, `effective_budget(cfg.session, HR.detect(os.environ))` returns `1000` instead of `500`. The reported `StartCost.budget` is therefore wrong for that session, and the doctor line can incorrectly say no OVER against the session's actual 500-token claude cap. The session target should be taken from `agent` (the value also passed to `start_texts(repo, agent)`), not from the ambient process environment.

chunk_findings.detail: `new = '{}'` is a TOML string literal `"{}"`, not an empty TOML table. The change declares a table knob `session.context_budget` whose keys are intended to be `global` and agent-type names, but the upgrade record would set the default to a string. On a system applying this unreleased change with no existing `session.context_budget` key, lookups such as `session.context_budget.global` or `session.context_budget.claude` fail because the value is a string, not a mapping. Use `new = {}` for an empty table.

chunk_findings.detail: The test sets the two documented aliases to different values (`context_budget_tokens=0` and `context_budget["global"]=30000`) and then asserts `SC.effective_budget(s, "x") == 30000`. This contradicts the change intent that `[session].context_budget_tokens` and `[session.context_budget].global` are the same value and that effective budget is `min(context_budget_tokens, context_budget.<agent type>)`; for an unset target `"x"` the min of `0` and inherited `30000` is `0`. The test therefore enforces the undocumented precedence that the table global key overrides the global knob, or it will fail against a correct min implementation.

chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding 4 still holds. The renamed test still exercises the disputed case: `_session(context_budget_tokens=0, context_budget={"global": 30000, "claude": 25000})`, then asserts `SC.effective_budget(s, "claude") == 25000` and `SC.effective_budget(s, "x") == 30000`. The knob doc this commit adds says `global` is a second spelling of `context_budget_tokens` and “if both are set the smaller applies”; under that rule the two global spellings `0` and `30000` would resolve to `0`, so the effective claude budget would be `min(0, 25000) == 0` and unset `x` would be `0`, not the asserted `25000`/`30000`. Renaming the test and adding that phrase does not answer the original defect: the exact contradictory assertion remains.

chunk_findings.detail: The new fold still resolves the two documented global spellings by assignment, not by the “if both are set the smaller applies” rule. Given TOML written with `[session] context_budget_tokens = 500` followed by `[session.context_budget] global = 800`, the table key is applied after the scalar key, so `_fold_budget_global` executes `target.context_budget_tokens = value.pop("global")` and overwrites `500` with `800`. The final session has `context_budget_tokens=800` and no table `global`, so `effective_budget` returns `800`, whereas the documented smaller-applies behavior is `500`. The outcome is therefore dependent on the order the two alias keys are applied.

chunk_findings.detail: The added assertion expects `SC.effective_budget(_session(context_budget_tokens=0, context_budget={"global": 30000}), "x") == 30000`. This contradicts the stated rule that `[session].context_budget_tokens` and `[session.context_budget].global` are the same global ceiling and the effective budget is `min(context_budget_tokens, context_budget.<agent type>)`. With the two global spellings set to `0` and `30000`, the smaller applies, so an unset type `"x"` inherits `30000`, and `min(0, 30000)` is `0`, not `30000`. This ratchet test therefore locks in the same wrong behavior from the prior confirmed finding and will force the implementation to violate the intended per-agent budget layering.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new fold operation does not enforce the documented “smaller applies” alias semantics when both spellings of the global budget are present in the same config layer. `_fold_budget_global` copies `[session.context_budget].global` into `context_budget_tokens` only while the table key is being assigned; a later assignment of `session.context_budget_tokens` in the same layer overwrites it (or the reverse, depending on layer key iteration order). Concrete input:

```toml
[session]
context_budget_tokens = 50000
[session.context_budget]
global = 10000
```

If the table key is processed before the scalar key, `target.context_budget_tokens` is first folded to `10000` and then overwritten to `50000`; the effective global becomes `50000`, above the `10000` declared as the smaller global. The loader still lets one spelling silently win instead of applying the smaller value.

chunk_findings.detail: The previous confirmed alias-conflict issue still holds. `context_budget_problem` is attached only to the `context_budget` table and therefore never sees the scalar `context_budget_tokens`. Input `[session] context_budget_tokens = 10000` plus `[session.context_budget] global = 50000` passes this check, but the knob doc in this same diff says `global` is “another spelling of `context_budget_tokens`: the same value.” The “later layer’s spelling winning” rule does not resolve a same-layer conflict, so the operator gets two different global ceilings and no validation error; if `config.py` later folds one into the other, that fold is not declared by this section’s check or doc.

chunk_findings.detail: `report` is where the doctor line is produced, but this diff never passes the new per-target budgets into `measure`. `measure` now accepts `targets` and defaults it to `{}`, and `StartCost.__str__` prints target lines only from `self.targets`; however `report` is not modified to call `effective_budget`/`configured_targets`, so `report(...).targets` is always empty. Concrete failure: with `[session] context_budget_tokens = 100000` and `[session.context_budget] claude = 20000`, `report(repo, cfg, "claude", start_texts).notes()` emits the global line but no `claude: N tokens (budget 20000)` line, so the per-agent doctor reporting required by the change is silently absent.

chunk_findings.detail: The new test codifies that `context_budget_tokens=0` with `context_budget={"claude": 0}` yields an effective budget of `0`, and that `context_budget_tokens=0` with `{"claude": 15000}` yields `codex == 0`. This contradicts this same file's line 7 and the knob doc: `0` means “no ceiling at that level,” and an unset type inherits the global. In the second scenario `codex` inherits the global `0`, so the global setting says “no global ceiling,” yet the effective budget becomes a zero-token budget for every unset type. The operator input `context_budget_tokens=0` plus only `claude=15000` gives claude a 15000 budget while all other agent types are reported as `(budget 0)` and flagged OVER for any non-empty startup text, even though the documented meaning of the global `0` is no ceiling rather than a zero-token limit.
